name: 2 Chronicles
v: So Solomon broke ground on the House of the LORD in Jerusalem, on Mount Moriah, where the LORD had appeared to his father David — the very spot David had prepared on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
Construction began on the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.
These are the foundations Solomon laid for the House of God: ninety feet long and thirty feet wide, measured by the old standard.
The portico across the front matched the width of the house — thirty feet — and rose thirty feet high. Inside, he overlaid it with pure gold.
The main hall he paneled with cypress, plated it with fine gold, and embossed it with palm trees and chains.
He studded the house with precious stones for sheer beauty, and the gold was gold from Parvaim.
He sheathed the whole structure in gold — beams, thresholds, walls, doors — and carved cherubim into the walls.
Then he built the Most Holy Place: thirty feet long, matching the width of the house, and thirty feet wide. He overlaid it with six hundred talents of pure gold —
the nails alone weighed fifty shekels of gold. The upper rooms he likewise covered in gold.
In the Most Holy Place he sculpted two cherubim and overlaid them with gold.
Their wings stretched thirty feet across: one wing of the first cherub touched the wall, seven and a half feet out; its other wing, also seven and a half feet, met the wing of the second cherub.
The second cherub matched it — one wing touching the far wall, the other reaching to meet its companion in the center.
So the wings of these cherubim spread thirty feet wide. They stood on their feet, faces turned toward the hall.
He hung the veil — blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen — and worked cherubim into it.
Out in front of the house he raised two pillars, fifty-two feet tall, each crowned with a capital seven and a half feet high.
He fashioned chains like a necklace and set them on the capitals, then made a hundred pomegranates and hung them in the chains.
He stood the pillars before the temple, one on the right and one on the left. The right one he named Jachin — *He establishes.* The left one, Boaz — *In him is strength.*

com.d:
# A Dwelling Place for God's Presence

When Solomon sets out to build God's house, he constructs far more than a building—he creates a sacred space where heaven and earth meet. The extravagant detail recorded in 2 Chronicles 3 reveals something profound about how God's people honor Him and what it costs to welcome His presence into their midst.

The temple's dimensions, materials, and appointments overflow with significance. Every specification—the length, the overlaid gold, the carved cherubim, the crimson curtains—speaks of intentionality and excellence devoted to God. Solomon doesn't cut corners or settle for adequacy. He gathers the finest cedar, covers surfaces with precious metal, and positions holy furnishings with careful precision. This wasn't wasteful extravagance but worshipful investment. When we build something for someone we love, we give our best. Solomon understood that the house of God deserves nothing less than the full expression of a nation's wealth, skill, and devotion.

Yet beneath the architectural specifics lies a tender invitation for us. Though we no longer build physical temples, the principle persists: God desires a dwelling place among His people. Peter reminds us that we are "living stones" being built into a spiritual house. Our own hearts, our families, our churches become the temples where God's presence dwells. This means the care Solomon lavished on Solomon's temple should mirror the care we invest in cultivating spaces—spiritual and relational—where God feels welcome.

The question that echoes through these detailed descriptions is personal and searching: What are we building with our lives? Are we constructing something grand enough, beautiful enough, worthy enough to house the Holy Spirit? Do our priorities, our time, our resources reflect that we believe God's presence is worth extraordinary investment?

Consider: What would it look like to devote your finest efforts—not to self-advancement or comfort—but to creating a dwelling place for God's presence in your own heart and home?
com.s:
The third chapter of Second Chronicles marks a pivotal transition in the Chronicler's narrative, moving from David's preparations to Solomon's actual construction of the temple. The Chronicler, writing in the post-exilic period (likely fifth or fourth century BCE), here emphasizes the theological continuity between the Davidic promise and its fulfillment, presenting Solomon as the divinely appointed builder who brings to fruition what his father could only envision.

The chapter opens by identifying Mount Moriah as the temple site, a geographical designation unique to Chronicles among the historical books. This location carries profound theological weight, connecting Solomon's temple to the narrative of Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac in Genesis 22. The Hebrew term *Môrîyâh* likely derives from the root *r'h* ("to see" or "to appear"), suggesting a place of divine manifestation. By invoking this patriarchal tradition, the Chronicler roots the temple's sanctity in Israel's deepest covenantal memory.

The architectural specifications provided reveal sophisticated ancient Near Eastern building practices. The cubit measurements given—sixty cubits in length and twenty in breadth—reflect the long cubit standard, though scholars debate whether the Chronicler employed the royal Egyptian cubit or a shorter Mesopotamian measurement. The term *'ûlām* (vestibule or porch) designates the entrance hall characteristic of Syrian temple architecture, suggesting cultural exchanges across the Levant.

Particularly significant is the Chronicler's attention to the gold overlay and the cherubim in the Most Holy Place. The verb *ṣāphâ* ("to overlay" or "to plate") appears repeatedly, emphasizing the temple's splendor as befitting the divine dwelling. The cherubim, spanning twenty cubits with outstretched wings touching both walls and meeting in the center, represent throne guardians common in ancient Near Eastern iconography, symbolizing God's sovereign presence.

The chapter's relationship to the parallel account in 1 Kings 6 presents interpretive challenges, as the Chronicler omits certain details while adding others, particularly the Moriah reference. This selective presentation reflects the Chronicler's distinctive theological agenda: presenting the temple as the legitimate center of Yahwistic worship for the restored post-exilic community, grounding their contemporary practice in sacred antiquity.
com.p:
Solomon's construction of the temple, recorded here in 2 Chronicles 3, occurred approximately 966 BC, roughly one thousand years before the incarnation of Christ. This chapter stands at the apex of Israel's golden age, during the united monarchy when David's son fulfilled the divine mandate his father received but could not complete. On the redemptive timeline, we have passed through Creation, Fall, Abraham's covenant, the Exodus deliverance, and the wilderness wandering. Israel now dwells in the Promised Land under her greatest king, and the kingdom reaches its zenith of glory and peace. The temple's construction marks the culmination of centuries of anticipation—the portable tabernacle of the wilderness finally becoming a permanent dwelling for Yahweh among His covenant people.

The location carries immense typological weight. Mount Moriah, where Solomon built, is the very place where Abraham raised the knife over Isaac before God provided the ram. That ancient altar of near-sacrifice now becomes the site where countless sacrifices will point forward to the Lamb of God. The threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, purchased by David during the plague, speaks of judgment halted by substitutionary offering. Every stone laid on this summit whispers of Calvary.

The architectural details overflow with prophetic significance. The cherubim overshadowing the Most Holy Place, their wings spanning the entire width of the inner sanctuary, recall Eden's guardians who barred humanity from God's presence after the Fall. Yet here they stand not as barriers but as attendants to the mercy seat, suggesting that a way back into divine fellowship has been opened through sacrifice. The veil separating the Holy Place from the Most Holy—that same veil torn from top to bottom when Christ breathed His last—stood for centuries as testimony that full access to God remained future.

The gold overlaying cedar, the bronze pillars named Jachin and Boaz ("He establishes" and "In Him is strength"), the precise measurements echoing cosmic order—all declare that this house, though glorious, was but a shadow of the true temple. Jesus Himself would stand in Herod's reconstruction of this very building and announce, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up," speaking of His body.

The church now lives as living stones in the temple Christ is building, awaiting the New Jerusalem where no temple exists because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple forever.
